national.title: A second judge blocks Trump's arch, saying it's unlikely to succeed in court
national.summary: A federal judge in Virginia said she will issue a preliminary injunction against Trump's arch, going a step further than the D.C. federal judge who temporarily blocked construction earlier this week.
national.body:
President Trump holds up a model of his proposed triumphal arch at a White House event in Oct. 2025. Two different federal judges have ruled against it this week. John McDonnell/AP hide caption

A federal judge in Virginia plans to issue a preliminary injunction blocking President Trump's triumphal arch indefinitely.

District Judge Leonie Brinkema said during a Friday hearing that she would grant the request of the county board of Arlington, Va., which sued over the arch in October. Democracy Forward, the nonprofit representing the plaintiffs, confirmed the ruling in a statement shared with NPR.

"We are pleased that the court has recognized the irreparable harm that will come to people who live and work in Arlington and stopped the massive vanity project while our case is heard and considered by the court," said senior counsel Kate Talmor.

Politics Judges have put Trump's arch and golf course on hold, but only for a matter of days The 250-foot arch would be built in Memorial Circle, which is part of D.C. but sits on the Virginia side of the Potomac River, a short distance from both Arlington National Cemetery and Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, both in Arlington.

Arlington County has argued that the arch would "cause significant harm" to its residents in multiple ways, including increasing noise and air pollution and "clogging thoroughfares needed for emergency transport services." And it said an arch that doubles as a military complex — as Trump has suggested — would pose public safety risks and require additional county resources to manage.

Arlington also argues the arch would disrupt historic sightlines between Arlington National Cemetery and D.C.'s National Mall , and pose logistical challenges for the roughly 24 to 27 funerals the cemetery holds every weekday. The county also has concerns about air and road traffic, saying construction-related delays could cause more accidents and disrupt emergency vehicles far beyond the traffic circle.

"In the last 60 days, Arlington police, fire, and emergency units have responded to approximately 200 incidents in the area surrounding the Circle, including traffic stops and assisting with unconscious persons within Arlington National Cemetery," they wrote. "And the visitors the Arch is intended to attract will increase demand for those same emergency services."

national.title: Travelers' concerns spike as Thanksgiving nears and tech hiccups grow, but few are dissuaded
national.summary: Just like bad weather, air travel disruptions irritate many Americans while dissuading comparatively few.
national.body:
Deepti Hajela, Associated Press Deepti Hajela, Associated Press

NEW YORK (AP) — At this point, it's practically as much of a Thanksgiving tradition as turkey and stuffing — crowded airports, long lines, jam-packed flights, the ever-present worry about delays and cancellations and extra expenses.

And for 2026's busy holiday travel week, which effectively begins Friday, there's another ingredient now: new concerns about the possibility of disruption and chaos when it comes to air-travel infrastructure in the wake of a rare nationwide ground stop last week — the longest since 9/11 — and a separate airline outage a few days later. Not to mention other, non-air-travel outages and tech problems that are causing nails to be bitten and hair to be pulled across the nation.

The thought of the potential travel problems is enough to make Tracey Evers feel iffy about whether she should continue with her plans to fly to the Caribbean this weekend to see her mother for the upcoming week or not, because she has things to take care of and getting stuck away from home would be a hassle. She's pretty sure she's not the only one.

"For a lot of people, especially as they're paying attention and because it's in the news where they're tying together all of the IT-based infrastructure challenges we're having ... I think more and more people are now getting anxious," said Evers, of Raleigh, North Carolina, an executive in the energy industry whose work requires frequent travel.

It's an anxiety fueled by the past 10 days' tech failures across industries and government — for airlines and in other sectors. But it's a familiar one, too.

Americans are no strangers to complaining about flying. They have been doing so in different ways for decades as air travel grew into a staple of American life. And it's one they're likely going to find a way to deal with for as long as it remains so, as seen in examples like the resurgence of air travel following the COVID pandemic.

But, just like bad weather, it irritates many Americans while dissuading comparatively few.

national.title: Indian man sentenced to 19-plus years in plot to assassinate US-based Sikh separatist leader
national.summary: Nikhil Gupta pleaded guilty to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering in February.
national.body:
A federal judge sentenced an Indian man to 235 months, more than 19 years, in an attempted plot to kill a leading Sikh political figure in the US.

Nikhil Gupta, an Indian national, pleaded guilty to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering in February. On Friday, the judge said he likely will be deported or removed after his sentence.

US prosecutors alleged Gupta was directed by an Indian government official to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a leading figure of the Khalistan movement, which advocates for an independent homeland for Sikhs.

India has denied involvement. Its government has accused Pannun of being a terrorist, which he denies.

Pannun, an American citizen, is the spokesman for US-based Sikh separatist group Sikhs for Justice (SFJ), banned in India since 2019. He previously told the BBC, "Nikhil Gupta's guilty plea was judicial confirmation that India's Modi government orchestrated a structured murder-for-hire assassination plot on American soil".

India has opposed the Khalistan movement, and its political parties also remain opposed to the matter. Sikhs are a religious minority that make up about 2% of India's population. Some groups have long called for a separate homeland for Sikhs.

Prosecutors alleged that in May 2023, Gupta was recruited by Vikash Yadav, an Indian intelligence officer, to carry out an assassination of Pannun.

Yadav allegedly provided Gupta with personal information about Pannun, including his address in New York and information about his daily activities, prosecutors said.

national.title: Maps and charts show record number of measles cases in U.S. this year
national.summary: CBS News has been tracking a record number of measles cases and outbreaks around the country in 2026. The majority of cases are among those who haven't been vaccinated.
national.body: So far in 2026, the U.S. has recorded the most measles cases in more than three decades as outbreaks spread in multiple states, according to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. By mid-July, the number had already surpassed all of 2025, which had been the worst year in recent history with more than 2,200 confirmed cases. By November, the number of cases topped 5,000, more than double the previous year's total.The ongoing outbreaks resulted in the U.S. losing its official measles elimination status, which it had held since 2000. "It's profoundly sad and disappointing," Dr. William Schaffner, a professor of preventive medicine and infectious diseases at the Vanderbilt University Medical Center, told CBS News. "What a tragedy. We have had children die of measles this past year. That should never have happened. Those deaths and all those cases, 5,000-plus, were completely preventable."In August, health officials in Pennsylvania reported the state's first two deaths connected to measles in 35 years. Several more deaths associated with measles were later reported as the state's outbreak surged, and deaths were also reported in New York and Wisconsin.Measles is one of the most contagious of all infectious diseases. In some cases, it can cause severe infections in the lungs and brain that can lead to cognitive issues, deafness or death. But it can be prevented by vaccination, which medical research has proven to be safe and highly effective.The CBS News data team has tracked confirmed measles cases nationwide as new data is released by state health departments and the CDC. Out of the 2,289 confirmed cases in 2025, more than 750 were connected to an outbreak in West Texas that led to the deaths of two children. Prior to 2025, the highest number of confirmed cases in the U.S. in recent years was 1,274 in 2019, driven by outbreaks in New York, California and Washington state. Most years, the total was much lower. Health experts point to lower vaccination rates as the main reason for increases in preventable infectious diseases like measles. The vast majority of cases have been in people who were unvaccinated, and outbreaks have spread in communities with lower vaccination rates.CDC data shows about 92.4% of kindergartners in the U.S. got their measles-mumps-rubella shots in the 2025-2026 school year, down slightly from 92.5% the previous year. national.title: Marine Corps hero under federal investigation
national.summary: Retired Sgt. Maj. Bradley Kasal, whose bloodied visage was depicted in an iconic Iraq War photo, is under investigation stemming from his tenure as a high school JROTC instructor.
national.body: Henderson, Nevada — One of the most celebrated Marine Corps veterans, whose heroism during the Iraq War earned him the nation's second-highest award for combat valor and a place in military history, is the subject of a criminal investigation over allegations stemming from his tenure as a high school instructor for a Junior Reserve Officers' Training Corps, CBS News has learned. Retired Sgt. Maj. Bradley Kasal, who served in the Marine Corps for 34 years, is under investigation by the Naval Criminal Investigative Service, the primary federal law enforcement agency for matters involving the Navy and Marine Corps. The allegations against the highly decorated Marine veteran have not been disclosed by the law enforcement agency. However, federal agencies told CBS News that the investigation concerns the period of time when he worked as a JROTC instructor at the Basic Academy of International Studies. The academy is a public high school in Henderson, Nevada, operated by the Clark County School District. The federal investigation marks a dramatic turn for a Marine whose actions on the battlefield made him a symbol of military courage. Kasal's heroism was captured in a 2004 photograph showing him in the Second Battle of Fallujah. His uniform was soaked in blood, and he was being helped out of a building by two Marines. His right leg was shattered, and his body riddled with gunshot wounds and grenade fragments, but he still gripped a pistol and combat knife. The scene was later immortalized in statues installed at two Marine bases. He retired after 34 years of service and was the recipient of two Purple Hearts and the Navy Cross, the second-highest decoration for combat valor, behind the Medal of Honor.On Wednesday, the Marine Corps told CBS News that the service is "aware of the allegations against a retired Marine Sergeant Major which occurred while he was employed as a civilian JROTC instructor by the Basic Academy of International Studies." The Marine Corps also said that the Naval Criminal Investigative Service "is actively investigating the allegations, as the Department of the Navy's lead for felony-level criminal investigations." national.title: Anthropic shares fall after blockbuster opening as wider tech sell-off continues
national.summary: Other tech companies have also taken a hit as share markets broadly slump.
national.body:
Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off deepens.

The fall in tech stocks continued to weigh on markets, with the S&P 500 down more than 2% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average down 0.7% by lunchtime.

Both US indexes touched correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index also fell more than 3.4% by the middle of trading on Friday.

Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping more than 12% to about $85 by lunchtime, close to its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83.

The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50.

The maker of the Claude chatbot raised a record $81bn in its initial public offering (IPO), but its share price moved significantly in the first day of trading.

The shares peaked at $115 on Thursday, before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.

national.title: Mamdani sets plan to close NYC's notorious Rikers Island jail by 2032
national.summary: The mayor unveiled the plan as the city is all but certain to blow past a legal requirement to close Rikers and replace it with four smaller, more modern jails by 2027.
national.body:
Anthony Izaguirre, Associated Press Anthony Izaguirre, Associated Press

NEW YORK (AP) — New York City's Rikers Island jail complex would close by 2032 under a sweeping plan announced Friday by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, whose strategy for finally shuttering the notorious facility hinges on substantially reducing the number of people kept behind bars.

The mayor, a Democrat, unveiled the plan as the city is all but certain to blow past a legal requirement to close Rikers and replace it with four smaller, more modern jails by 2027.

For years, Rikers Island has stood as a symbol of dysfunction, with the network of jails so plagued by violence and overcrowding that a federal judge, citing " abnormal and unacceptable " conditions, appointed an outside manager to restore order and implement reforms.

Mamdani has been a vocal proponent of closing Rikers, though the longstanding plan to build new jails has met fierce pushback, including from his predecessor, former Mayor Eric Adams, who opposed federal oversight and borough jails.

At a celebratory news conference at City Hall, Mamdani said the extended timeline was needed because of resistance from the previous administration, calling Rikers "a place we have long turned our eyes away from rather than confront head on."

"The call to close Rikers has echoed across our city for decades. Work has begun to do so, then stopped, then started once again. What will make this chapter different is our commitment to see it through," he said.

The plan centers on a goal of lowering the city's inmate population from the around 6,700 people currently housed at Rikers to a little over 4,000.

national.body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani unveiled his strategy to shut down Rikers Island and replace it with four smaller jails across the city.The city is legally required to close the troubled jail complex by August 2027. Mamdani acknowledges the city won't meet that deadline, and is now proposing a closure date of 2032, along with a sweeping overhaul of how the city handles people awaiting trial. The six-year plan requires legislative approval. The administration closed one Rikers facility earlier this year, but the rest of the complex remains open."I'm proud to say New York City will close Rikers Island once and for all," Mamdani said. The four new borough-based jails are designed to hold about 4,100 people. That's far fewer than the roughly 6,700 people reported in custody at Rikers in June. Under Mamdani's plan, the first replacement jail won't open until 2029."The first jail will open in Brooklyn in 2029, followed by Bronx and Queens 2031, Manhattan 2032. These jails will look and feel very different than Rikers," Mamdani said. "It is about creating a system grounded in dignity. In the meantime, his administration is putting millions toward reducing the jail population and improving conditions. The plan announced Friday includes $50 million for job training, education, mental health counseling and drug treatment. national.title: Trump initially accepted the midterm results, but most GOP voters doubt they were fair
national.summary: Less than half of Republicans nationwide considered the midterm elections "free and fair," according to new polling.
national.body:
President Trump may have initially accepted the results of his party's midterm losses , but data released Friday shows there is still broad distrust in the elections process among Republicans.

Less than half of Republican voters nationwide considered the midterm elections "free and fair," according to new polling by the University of California San Diego. Just 52% of Republicans said they trusted votes were counted accurately.

In comparison, after the 2024 election that Trump won, more than 80% of Republicans said they had confidence in the vote-counting process.

While trust in elections often dips for voters of the losing party, the GOP has seen bigger swings in confidence in recent years, as Trump has falsely claimed that U.S. elections are corrupt.

"There are still a lot of people who remain unconvinced that they can trust elections," said Thad Kousser, a co-director of UC San Diego's Center for Transparent and Trusted Elections. "And they're predominantly located in one [political] party."

Overall, a wide majority — 66% — of Americans said they think the midterms were fair. That represents an improvement from before the election , when less than half of U.S. adults said they expected free and fair contests.

But that post-election increase in trust was buoyed by Democrats and independents — many of whom worried before Election Day about potential federal interference at the polls that didn't come to pass .

"It would be a mistake to [look at the 66%] and think, 'Oh, everyone has a pretty good view of the election,'" said Lauren Prather, also a co-director of UC San Diego's election center. "It really buries the lede a little bit about the partisan gap."

national.summary: Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.
national.body:
Poland says a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.

Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.

Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during one of its biggest aerial attacks on Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022.

Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the Kh-101 missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec in southeastern Poland about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.

The cruise missile, designed for precision targets, crashed at about 06:30 (5:30GMT) and Natalie Szponar, a local resident, said she was getting her children ready for school when she heard a "whistle and a dull impact".

The moment of impact was caught by a camera on a farm, and officials later made clear there was no risk to residents.

Another suspected missile went down near Rudnik nad Sanem to the west of Nowy Lipowiec, and a jet-powered drone crashed to the south near Mołodycz, said Kosiniak-Kamysz.

He called the incursion into Polish airspace a "provocation" from Russia and said he would be asking Nato for additional support.

The outbreak was then reported days later on Nov. 15.At least 134 of 2,936 passengers and 14 of the 1,132 crew members have reported symptoms such as vomiting and diarrhea, according to the CDC.In response to the outbreak, Princess Cruises and the crew on board the ship said there have been increased cleaning and disinfection efforts according to their outbreak and response plan.In addition, passengers and crew who are sick have been isolated."Norovirus is often the cause of gastrointestinal illness outbreaks on cruise ships, but we don't always know the cause of the outbreak when we begin an investigation," the CDC said on its website. Ashley Branch, Orchestra Noir's operations manager, hurriedly completes her final tasks before curtain call at the Warner Theater in Washington, D.C. It is two hours before the ensemble's Saturday night concert and her main goal is simple: plan to deal with whatever she didn't plan for.

The D.C. show comes partway through the ensemble's 20-city The Culture 2000s tour, which has taken the group to cities like Jacksonville and Philadelphia.

Founded in 2016 by music director Jason Ikeem Rodgers, the all-Black Atlanta-based orchestra performs classic hits spanning the genres of jazz, blues and R&B. "I wore every single hat there was to wear," Keisha told NPR. "It was just very day-to-day. I mean, every little thing you could think of operationally was me."

But over the last decade, Orchestra Noir has expanded to 23 musicians and a leadership staff of four people. The orchestra averages about 20 shows per tour.

national.title: Myanmar is the first state found responsible for genocide. Here's how the ICJ ruled in other cases
national.summary: The International Court of Justice has been asked to reach that conclusion before, but never found enough evidence to make the determination of a state-sponsored genocide like the one targeting the Rohingya.
national.body:
THE HAGUE, Netherlands (AP) — The United Nations' top court has for the first time ruled that a nation committed what legal scholars call the crime of crimes, finding that Myanmar committed genocide in a brutal 2017 military crackdown against the Rohingya minority.

The International Court of Justice has been asked to reach that conclusion before, but never found enough evidence to make the determination of a state-sponsored genocide like the one targeting the Rohingya.

WATCH: International Court of Justice finds Myanmar guilty of genocide against Rohingya

The World Court has more cases on its docket dealing with alleged breaches of the 1948 Genocide Convention, including a politically charged case about Israel's actions in Gaza.

What happened: The Srebrenica massacre was a peak in the violence of Bosnia's 1992-95 war, which came after the breakup of Yugoslavia unleashed nationalist passions and territorial ambitions across the region.

On July 11, 1995, Serbs overran Srebrenica, at the time a U.N.-protected safe area. They separated at least 8,000 Bosniak men and boys from their wives, mothers and sisters and slaughtered them. Those who tried to escape were chased through the woods and over the mountains around town.

How the court ruled: The court, basing itself in part on verdicts at a United Nations war crimes tribunal, said in a 2007 ruling that the Srebrenica killings amounted to genocide. However, it did not find Serbia responsible. It did find Serbia had violated its obligation to prevent genocide. That obligation is enshrined in the 1948 Genocide Convention.

What happened: In another war that erupted out of the messy breakup of Yugoslavia, Serb forces attacked several regions of neighboring Croatia, killing and wounding Croat citizens. Croatia accused Serbia of controlling forces responsible for attacks from 1991-95 that Zagreb said amounted to genocide.

national.title: New UFO files show contractor planned vault for "exotic material"
national.summary: The Pentagon's latest batch of UFO files includes a report from a government contractor detailing plans for an underground vault to store "exotic material or tissue" it was seeking.
national.body: Washington — The Pentagon released a new batch of UFO files on Friday, including one report from a government contractor detailing plans for an underground vault to store "exotic material or tissue" and recovered "hardware" it hoped to obtain.The report was among 43 files included in the eighth release of UFO, or UAP, documents. The records mostly consisted of historical documents from the Air Force and CIA dating from the 1950s, with others describing more recent events.What's in the new UFO files?The July 2009 report was produced by Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies as part of a Defense Intelligence Agency program, funded by Congress at the urging of then-Sen. Harry Reid, to study potential future aerospace threats.The 538-page document said the company identified the need for "a highly secure underground vault" to store "hardware and biological samples from the corporate world and/or from private individuals and groups located elsewhere, including Brazil." It would be located in Nevada."It was recognized by the BAASS administrator that there was no highly secure facility at BAASS to store exotic material or tissue that the organization could obtain," the report said. "Accordingly, the BAASS administrator designed an underground facility to be located in North Las Vegas at the Bigelow Aerospace facility."The facility would be buried under 15 to 20 feet of dirt and feature a 5,000-square-foot vault with "3 foot thick walls" and a thick steel door. "Any surface structures protruding from the ground will be extensively camouflaged," the report said.There's no public record that the vault was ever built. national.body:
Nearly 600 women were killed in South Africa between July and September this year, according to the country's latest crime statistics.

This figure includes 13 women whose partially naked and bruised bodies were found dumped in public areas in and around Johannesburg.

The murders triggered national outrage and police faced pressure to find the culprits, in a country with one of the highest rates of gender-based violence and murder rates in the world.

In the latest shocking killing, five women and a toddler were gunned down in Free State province earlier this week.

The latest crime statistics, released on Friday, revealed that 581 women were killed in the country between July and September, including 131 in the Gauteng province which includes Johannesburg.

The same statistics revealed a slight decline in the number of murders.

Police reported 5,590 murders, 204 fewer than in the same period last year. This still come to an average of about 60 murders a day.

It is not clear whether the number of women killed is an increase or decrease because the police had stopped giving these figures recently due to what they said were "significant anomalies" in the statistics.

Zeta-Jones, who is married to Michael Douglas, son of Hollywood star Kirk, previously said the "nepo baby" term was "horrific" . It refers to children of famous parents perceived to have achieved riches and success off their parents' backs.

But the young actor said her parents taught her to build her "own identity" and she has learned how to deal with the "pressure".

During an interview with Elle Spain, Carys Douglas said her parents "do not hide" from her that people would have preconceived ideas about her.

"They taught me that building my own identity depended on me and no one else. It was my responsibility, and it still is.

"As time has gone on, I've come to understand that there are different ways to deal with that kind of pressure," she said.

Her father, star of hit 1980s films such as Wall Street and Fatal Attraction, recently stated that he is not a fan of the "nepo baby" label, calling it an "unfortunate title".

national.title: Iran war has permanently reshaped energy priorities, IEA report says
national.summary: The repercussions from the Iran war will "leave lasting marks" on the world's energy sector, said the Paris-based IEA, founded after the 1973-74 oil crisis.
national.body:
Anton L. Delgado, Associated Press Anton L. Delgado, Associated Press

The greatest energy shock in history and growing climate change concerns are reshaping how the world will power homes , drive cars and fuel industries, said an International Energy Agency report released Thursday.

The repercussions from the Iran war will "leave lasting marks" on the world's energy sector, said the Paris-based IEA, founded after the 1973-74 oil crisis.

Energy-hungry nations will prioritize the security and affordability of their electricity, the report said, which will benefit renewable technologies, like solar energy, and other alternatives, like nuclear power. But it also reinforces the case to keep coal as a backup for times of crisis.

This is especially true in coal-rich Asia, which went into energy triage when the Iran war cut off the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow passageway where about a fifth of the world's traded oil flowed.

The report looks "past the current turmoil to explore the range of energy futures that could emerge from today's upheaval," said IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol, who warned that "the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper the effects will be."

"I don't see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before," he said.

The annual United Nations climate talks in Turkey, known as COP31, are in their final week. Before these negotiations, the U.N. announced the world is dangerously close to missing its goal of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures.

national.title: Trump holds press conference after meeting with Xi and Putin
national.summary: Trump did not formally take questions while in China at the end of his trip, though it's typically expected on presidential foreign trips.
national.body:
President Trump touted his recent trip to Asia where he met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin during a White House press conference Friday, saying the U.S. took the stage from a position of strength.

"The United States entered this trip from a position of unmatched economic and diplomatic strength," he said, though the historic summit between the three countries yielded few tangible results.

Trump, flanked by Vice President Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, noted that oil prices have been dropping and noted that those prices are closely tied to how things are going in Iran.

"They want to make a deal, but they don't want to make a deal that's acceptable to me. We want to make a real deal, not a fake deal that they've been doing for 51 years," he said.

Trump also said he and Chinese President Xi were agreeing to "joint guardrails" amid the race to develop artificial intelligence, a notable acknowledgement about the risks involved.

Trump, who said Xi also likes his term "super intelligence" rather than artificial, said, "Problem is, it may be too super. So, President Xi and I agree that we're going to do some joint guardrails, the two of us."

Trump added that he would continue to push for the construction of data centers in the U.S.

"Make them pay your community, but take advantage. Don't shut them off. And there's always somebody else in this country. But if it's not this country, there's somebody else outside. And we're not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country. We're not going to allow that to happen," Trump said.

national.title: Trump administration moves to have lawsuit dismissed in challenge to Alaska's U.S. Senate race
national.summary: In their filing, Justice Department attorneys urged the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to overturn the lower court's dismissal of the case to erase the loss, but then dismiss the case anyway.
national.body:
Nicholas Riccardi, Associated Press Nicholas Riccardi, Associated Press

Becky Bohrer, Associated Press Becky Bohrer, Associated Press

JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — The Trump administration on Thursday moved to effectively drop its lawsuit that sought to block the certification of Democrat Mary Peltola's victory in Alaska's U.S. Senate race, ending a much-criticized gambit by the president to prevent one of his political rivals from taking office.

Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News

The legal challenge centered around the presence on the ballot of a second candidate with the same name as the incumbent, Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. The Alaska Supreme Court already ruled that the second Sullivan's candidacy is legal and that he could be on the ballot.

Attorneys for the state, which is currently controlled by Republicans, also objected to the administration's move, calling it legally "meritless" and filing papers to help get the initial case dismissed. The administration moved Thursday to have an appeals court declare its case moot, two days after the race was decided.

In their filing, Justice Department attorneys urged the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to overturn the lower court's dismissal of the case to erase the loss, but then dismiss the case anyway. They said the court "should hold that this case is moot, vacate the underlying order, and remand for dismissal on that ground."

That decision comes after Peltola won an outright majority in the race to become Democrats' 56th senator, the ninth Senate pickup for the party in its midterm blowout. Peltola won by more votes than were taken by the other candidate, Dan J. Sullivan.

national.title: White House taps Kirsten Davies as cyber chief after outages rattle Americans
national.summary: The White House named a new national cyber director Thursday after a series of widespread service outages disrupted life and unnerved many Americans.
national.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The White House named a new national cyber director Thursday after a series of widespread service outages disrupted life and unnerved many Americans.

Kirsten Davies, chief information officer at the Defense Department, will fill the role, according to social media posts by several members of Trump's cabinet. She will replace Sean Cairncross as the administration's top cybersecurity official.

"Our nation stands in the crossroad of analog, digital, and quantum technologies, our American way of living increasingly interconnected," Davies wrote in a post on X. "Our opportunity is to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come … but only if we modernize and drive resilience into the foundations our great nation runs on, as well as build cyber talent for our future."

President Donald Trump faced a groundswell of criticism as Americans grappled with a cascade of service outages that snarled travel, cut off work, limited bank access and disrupted classified communications.

Even staunch Trump allies accused the administration of lying to Americans or hiding information about the true cause of the disruptions. Over the past week, Microsoft, Chase Bank, air traffic control and the National Security Agency have all been affected.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday sought to assure Americans that there's "zero" information that the technical failures are related to each other or to a malign actor.

The White House made the change as Trump returned from a three-day trip to Asia, where he downplayed the episodes, declaring that "things like that happen."

"She has proven herself to be a dedicated patriot and professional, and we are confident she will advance President Trump's America First agenda across the cybersecurity landscape," Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth wrote in a post on X congratulating Davies.

national.title: White House removes cyber-security chief after series of tech outages
national.summary: CBS is reporting he has been fired after losing the confidence of White House chief of staff Stephen Miller.
national.body:
The top cyber-security official in the US government is leaving his post after a little over a year in the job, US media report.

CBS, the BBC's US news partner, and other media report that White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross has been fired after losing the confidence of White House chief of staff Stephen Miller.

It comes after a string of tech outages which hit banking, air traffic control and other sectors.

US officials said the outages were not caused by cyberattacks but the blackouts had sparked scrutiny from members of Congress who demanded a clearer explanation of what went wrong.

There has been no official confirmation of the removal of Cairncross but Secretary of State Marco Rubio posted on X , external to say Department of Defense chief information officer Kirsten Davies was the new national cyber director.

The AFP news agency and CBS both said sources had told them Cairncross's sacking was supported by President Donald Trump. The BBC has asked the White House for comment.

The news, first reported by Axios , external , follows security concerns, including the ability of advanced AI models - mostly from US companies - to discover vulnerabilities which humans would not be able to find on their own.

Earlier this week, Rubio said there was "zero evidence" the outages were connected, adding "we are not under systemic attack".

national.summary: Two county prosecutors say the Trump administration broke the law when it exempted U.S. companies from ownership reporting.
national.body: In March 2025, a conservative comedian named Terrence K. Williams had a plea for Elon Musk: ask President Trump to scrap a "ridiculous" federal rule that forced companies to disclose their true owners."I'm begging you!" Williams posted on X, Musk's social media platform. "It's targeting conservatives and small businesses!"The billionaire replied, "I can look into it."A day later, the Trump administration took action. In a post on X, the Treasury Department announced it would no longer enforce penalties or fines against U.S. citizens, domestic companies or their owners under the law, known as the Corporate Transparency Act.Now, two local prosecutors are suing to stop the administration from erasing roughly 15 million company ownership records it has already collected, CBS News has learned.On Thursday, the top prosecutors in Hennepin County, Minnesota, and Pima County, Arizona — Mary Moriarty and Laura Conover — alleged in a lawsuit that the Treasury Department violated the law when it exempted American companies from the disclosure rules and let foreign companies leave out their American owners. Moriarty and Conover, both Democrats, say the ownership records would help their offices pursue cartel money laundering, wage theft, fraud and organized retail theft carried out through shell companies. The suit also names Attorney General Todd Blanche and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, whose departments had to sign off on the exemptions.Deleting the records would make it "easier than ever for criminals to use shell and front companies for illicit activities and evade detection," the lawsuit, filed in federal court in Washington, D.C., says. It argues that "because law enforcement cannot know in advance which companies will warrant scrutiny, the value of beneficial-ownership reporting lies in collecting that information before the need for it arises."In a statement to CBS News, a Treasury spokesperson said removing the reporting requirement was "a victory for common sense," adding that the department made the change "after careful consideration of the costs to small business owners and the benefit to national security." national.summary: Rockstar Games ended a 13-year wait with what is expected to be the biggest entertainment launch ever.
national.body:
Grand Theft Auto 6 is estimated to be the biggest entertainment launch in history after the blockbuster video game debuted on Thursday , following a 13-year wait.

Internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare said PS5 downloads in the UK peaked at 8.6 times normal levels around its launch. New Zealand, where GTA 6 was first available, saw a 14.8-fold spike four hours before, suggesting some players switched regions for early access .

Pre-orders and first-day sales totalled more than 24.5 million units, making about $2.36bn (£1.8bn), according to analytics site Sensor Tower.

In comparison, this year's highest-grossing movie so far, Spider-Man: Brand New Day, made $2.5bn over its entire run in cinemas .

GTA 6's maker Rockstar and parent company Take-Two have not released details of the game's sales but said demand has been "unprecedented". The BBC has contacted both firms for comment.

In its initial findings since the game's launch, Cloudflare also recorded a huge surge in traffic to Rockstar's online services, peaking at 11.2 times normal levels in Australia and 9.3 times in the US East Coast.

In Europe, UK interest was particularly strong, reaching seven times normal levels compared with 5.3 times in France and Germany.

The game is the latest instalment in Rockstar's nearly three decade old crime simulator franchise, which has become one of the most popular games in history .

national.title: Texas death-row inmate screams as execution takes more than one hour
national.summary: This prolonged execution comes weeks after Christa Pike survived the lethal injection of the same drug.
national.body:
A US death row inmate has screamed in apparent pain during his Texas execution which lasted more than an hour.

This is "not working the way it should be," Reinaldo Dennes, 70, said as he was being injected with the drug pentobarbital, according to witnesses.

A spokeswoman for the Texas Department of Criminal Justice said there had been unsuccessful attempts to find veins for the injections, but added that Dennes had reported pain in parts of his body where there were no attempted injections.

Dennes's case comes weeks after the botched execution of Christa Pike, who survived two lethal doses and is believed to be the only individual to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.

Dennes was sentenced to death over the 1996 murder of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer who was found shot multiple times.

His execution came on the same day another inmate was put to death in Florida.

Executions with a lethal drug usually last from a few minutes to over an hour.

Michael Graczyk, an Associated Press reporter who has witnessed many such executions, described how they had waited for an unusually long time before being taken into the chamber. According to him, such delays are usually due to an inmate resisting the procedure or difficulty in finding veins.

local.title: Wayne County supervisors appoint new health director
local.summary: The Board of Supervisors approved Jennifer Rodriguez’s appointment at its meeting this week.
local.body:
The Board of Supervisors approved Jennifer Rodriguez’s appointment at its meeting Tuesday morning.

Rodriguez currently is director of Livingston County Health, where she has served since 2013. She succeeds Diane Devlin, who retired in March. Deputy Director Kerry Van Auken has been directing the agency since Devlin’s retirement.

Rodriguez will be paid nearly $166,000. She starts her new position Jan. 4.

She said her decision to take the Wayne position “is rooted in my longstanding passion for public health and my commitment to improving the health and well-being of the communities I serve.”

Rodriguez said she oversaw multiple areas of public health and community services in Livingston County, “which provided me with invaluable leadership experience and a broader understanding of the challenges facing rural communities.” In October, she took on the additional role of interim director of community mental health services in Livingston County following the resignation of Sarah McCumiskey.

She explained that the Wayne County job allows her “to return my full attention to core public health services, preventive health care, and the essential work of improving population health outcomes.”

“At the heart of my decision is something very simple: I believe deeply in the power of prevention, the importance of accessible healthcare, and the ability of local public health departments to make a lasting difference in people’s lives,” Rodriguez continued. “I am grateful for my years in Livingston County and enthusiastic about beginning this next chapter serving the residents of Wayne County. … I am genuinely excited to join Wayne County, learn from its residents and community partners, and work alongside its dedicated public health professionals. I see this transition as an opportunity for both professional growth and a renewed focus on the work that first drew me to public health.”

Rodriguez was named a Women of Excellence honoree by the Rochester Business Journal in 2021. The RBJ said the program celebrates “high-achieving women across the Greater Rochester area for their professional accomplishments, community involvement, and commitment to mentoring.”

local.title: Langworthy again calls for natural-gas repowering of city plant
local.summary: An area representative is again making a push to have the former NRG plant repowered with natural gas. U.S. Rep. Nick Langworthy this week called on Gov. Kathy Hochul to immediately suspend implementation of New York’s All-Electric Buildings Act and work with the State Legislature to permanently rep
local.body:
An area representative is again making a push to have the former NRG plant repowered with natural gas.

U.S. Rep. Nick Langworthy this week called on Gov. Kathy Hochul to immediately suspend implementation of New York's All-Electric Buildings Act and work with the State Legislature to permanently repeal the law following a new warning from the New York Independent System Operator (NYISO) that the state is facing its first-ever projected statewide electricity resource deficiency. Langworthy also renewed his call to repurpose the shuttered Dunkirk coal plant for natural gas.

The Dunkirk location is now owned by Genover, which delivers infrastructure across transmission and distribution, substation, generation, engineering and fleet support -- through its own capabilities and a group of specialized operating companies. It also is being eyed as a potential nuclear site.

"This is a five-alarm warning for Governor Hochul and every legislator in Albany that their dangerous, reckless push to full electrification will have catastrophic consequences if allowed to go forward," said Langworthy. "The findings in this report detail the exact outcome I have been talking about since day one, and why I've fought to block this disastrous law from taking effect. The impact of their policies is no longer theoretical--the facts are at our front door and New Yorkers' safety and security is at grave risk."

According to NYISO's latest Reliability Needs Assessment, New York could face an electricity supply shortfall beginning in 2033, initially estimated at 225 megawatts and growing to more than 1,850 megawatts by 2036. The report underscores the growing strain on an aging electric grid, declining availability of existing power generation, and rising electricity demand.

Langworthy continued, "I am calling on Governor Hochul to permanently halt implementation of her natural gas ban and work with the legislature to officially repeal this misguided mandate. New York needs more reliable and affordable energy, not fewer options. Natural gas is an important part of our energy mix, and families, businesses, and builders should be able to choose the energy sources that make sense for their needs and budgets. Time is of the essence to get more supply into the system and while nuclear is a great part of the equation we can't afford the gaps while we wait for those plants to come online. That's exactly why repurposing the Dunkirk plant to natural gas makes perfect sense."

local.body:
Community Bank plans to close its Central Avenue branch in Dunkirk in the spring, consolidating its banking services at another location nearby.

In a letter dated Nov. 16, the bank informed customers its branch at 345 Central Ave. will close effective Friday, March 19. Banking services offered at that location will be transferred to the branch at 3909 Vineyard Drive in Dunkirk.

The bank said the decision followed a thorough assessment of its branch network and how it can best serve customers as banking needs evolve.

"We understand a branch closing may be inconvenient and we appreciate the trust you have placed in Community Bank," the letter stated. The bank also indicated its team would work to help customers navigate the transition.

According to the notification, customers’ existing accounts will remain unchanged. Account numbers, checks and ATM/debit cards will continue to function without interruption, and no action is required on the part of customers.

Community Bank also noted that customers will have access to surcharge-free ATMs through the Allpoint network, which includes more than 55,000 locations nationwide.

The bank encouraged customers who use the Central Avenue branch’s night depository to contact a branch representative before Feb. 12, to discuss access and arrangements at another location.

Customers who currently rent safe deposit boxes at the Central Avenue branch will be offered the opportunity to transfer to another Community Bank location where space is available. The bank said it would waive the charge for the first year. Customers are asked to contact a Central Avenue branch representative before Jan. 29, 2027, to make arrangements.

TURIN, Italy (AP) -- U.S. Open finalist Ben Shelton did his part. Then he got some help from top-ranked Alexander Zverev to advance at the ATP Finals.

Shelton twice aced his way out of trouble in the first-set tiebreaker and beat Rafael Jodar 7-6 (8), 7-5 on Thursday.

When Zverev beat Arthur Fils 6-4, 7-6 (6) later in the final match of the group, Shelton was secured a spot in the semifinals of the elite event for the season’s top eight players.

Shelton will face Carlos Alcaraz in the semifinals in another rematch of their U.S. Open quarterfinal that ended at 3:33 a.m.

While Shelton won that five-set clash in New York, Alcaraz recently got revenge in the Paris Masters final.

Alcaraz has an injury concern, though, after getting his left thigh strapped during a victory over Daniil Medvedev on Wednesday; and plays Flavio Cobolli in his final group match on Friday.

Zverev, who had already advanced and finished group play with a perfect three wins, will face either Medvedev or Frances Tiafoe -- who play Friday to determine the last semifinalist.

Zverev appeared to have an issue during the tiebreaker. He said afterward the problem is his ankle.

local.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — Rasmus Dahlin and Beck Malenstyn scored 25 seconds apart in the first period to chase Logan Thompson, and the Buffalo Sabres sent Washington to its fourth straight loss, beating the Capitals 6-3 on Thursday night. Jack Quinn scored twice — once into an empty net — and Zach Benson a
local.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) -- Rasmus Dahlin and Beck Malenstyn scored 25 seconds apart in the first period to chase Logan Thompson, and the Buffalo Sabres sent Washington to its fourth straight loss, beating the Capitals 6-3 on Thursday night.

Jack Quinn scored twice -- once into an empty net -- and Zach Benson and Tage Thompson also scored for the Sabres. Buffalo converted on five of its 13 shots in the first two periods. Alex Tuch, Ryan Leonard and Boone Jenner scored Washington, which has fallen to .500 after entering the season with lofty expectations.

Alex Ovechkin broke a tie with longtime teammate Nicklas Backstrom for Washington’s career lead in assists with his 763rd.

The Capitals have allowed at least five goals in four straight games and six of their last eight. On Wednesday it took them only two periods to do so. Thompson allowed three goals on five shots before being yanked in favor of Charlie Lindgren.

It was the second time in his last six starts Thompson was pulled early.

After Quinn opened the scoring, Dahlin entered the zone on a power play, and when Thompson overplayed him a bit to the near post, the Buffalo defenseman swooped behind the net and wrapped the puck into the vacated other side.

Tuch scored again against his former team. He had two goals against Buffalo, including the winner in overtime, in a game last month.

It was 4-1 after one Thursday, and Tage Thompson scored on the power play near the end of the second. Leonard scored to cap a dominant stretch on the power play for Washington in the third, then Jenner poked the puck in with 10:16 remaining after Buffalo goalie Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen seemed unaware it was loose.

local.title: Other voices: Air traffic system needs reforms
local.summary: And you thought flying in America couldn’t get worse. Then on Friday more than 12,000 flights were canceled after the Federal Aviation Administration ordered an extraordinary nationwide ground stop that lasted more than four hours. Was there a terrorist threat? Cyber-attack? No, the cause appears to
local.body:
And you thought flying in America couldn't get worse. Then on Friday more than 12,000 flights were canceled after the Federal Aviation Administration ordered an extraordinary nationwide ground stop that lasted more than four hours. Was there a terrorist threat? Cyber-attack? No, the cause appears to have been routine government failure.

Friday's fiasco, which disrupted millions of travel plans, laid bare the myriad dysfunctions of America's government-run air-traffic control system that have led to repeated system failures and delays. Flyers were left stranded for hours as the FAA tried to diagnose and fix the problem, which officials eventually tied to a new router at a facility in Arkansas.

According to FAA officials, the router along with another one in Texas flooded its communications system with data. It's far from reassuring that one or two malfunctioning devices can take down continental air traffic. Or that the Sherlock Holmeses at the FAA still aren't sure exactly what went wrong.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed either a faulty device or "incompetence" by the contractor L3Harris Technologies that had installed it. HPE, the router manufacturer, said its hardware "did not fail." While Mr. Duffy claimed the government hasn't found evidence of nefarious causes, it's understandable to wonder given that adversaries are stepping up cyberattacks across the U.S. economy and government.

As is their habit, politicians rushed to capitalize on the public misery. Democrats blamed the Administration's new SMART system, which uses AI to analyze airline schedules, weather, airspace conditions, among other things, to prevent flight conflicts that cause delays. There's no evidence the AI system contributed to Friday's problems.

Mr. Duffy on Thursday called for $30 billion in more funding, on top of the $12.5 billion Republicans appropriated in last year's tax bill. After Friday's failure, he raised the demand to $50 billion. But throwing more money at an unaccountable agency will at best be a temporary fix and will reward dysfunction.

In 2003 Congress directed the FAA to modernize America's aging air-traffic system, yet the Government Accountability Office reported in September that the FAA doesn't plan to complete the first phase of upgrades until December 2028. That's a quarter-century.

The GAO also said the FAA lacks a reliable estimate for when the second phase will be done and how much the entire project will cost. This is government incompetence across several administrations at a California bullet-train-to-nowhere level. Criticism from Pete Buttigieg, the Biden transportation secretary, is especially laughable given his obvious failure to improve things over four years in the job. And he apparently wants to run for President again.

local.summary: When Ty Harper took over as head coach at Chautauqua Lake/Westfield/Brocton a season ago, he arrived in Mayville with a stable of receiving options at his disposal. local.body:
When Ty Harper took over as head coach at Chautauqua Lake/Westfield/Brocton a season ago, he arrived in Mayville with a stable of receiving options at his disposal.

Devin Hewes would end up with 57 catches for 708 yards and six touchdowns and tight end Asher Olson had 39 catches for 642 yards and nine touchdowns while Nick Jacobson, a returning New York State Sportswriters Association Class C second-team all-star, battled injuries throughout the season.

A year later those three, in addition to third-leading receiver Carson Fairbank, were lost to graduation and the Eagles were left wondering who would fill the void.

"There was concern across the board. Anytime you have to replace nine guys on offense, that's a pretty big task," Harper said Tuesday evening. "When you couple having to replace all of those talented players with the fact that you're interjecting a sophomore into the most important position on the field. I would say there was probably some anxiety coming into the season."

Juniors Aiden Woodis and Ian Kindermann have answered the call, giving first-year sophomore starting quarterback Josh Swan reliable options in the passing game.

The aerial attack, which came through in two key instances a week ago, will likely be needed again at noon Saturday when Chautauqua Lake/Westfield/Brocton takes on Hornell/Arkport-Canaseraga in the Class C Far West Regional at SUNY Brockport's Bob Boozer Field at Eunice Kennedy Shriver Stadium.

Woodis has been more of a chain mover for the Eagles. He has 27 receptions for 288 yards and two scores on the year.

"He just made plays all the time. You get to see these guys in practice every day. The competitors really kind of separate themselves. You can tell when kids are competing all the time. Aiden just kind of had that characteristic from Day 1 last year in practice. We have jayvee in burgundy and varsity in navy; Aiden spent maybe five minutes in a red jersey before we told him to go put a navy jersey on," Harper said. "Aiden has been hampered by that knee injury from the state semifinals last year. He's going to need surgery at some point to repair his knee. He's gutting it out. To people who aren't there every day it might look like production is down, but he's doing a lot for us and is not close to 100%."

local.title: Ninety percent is not diversity of thought
local.summary: From previous years, you, faithful reader of this column, know what has happened. An organization legally separate from Chautauqua Institution and headquartered outside of the institution annually invites a speaker to the institution. More than 90 percent of the speakers over the years have been lib
local.body:
From previous years, you, faithful reader of this column, know what has happened. An organization legally separate from Chautauqua Institution and headquartered outside of the institution annually invites a speaker to the institution. More than 90 percent of the speakers over the years have been liberals.

Guess what? That's right. The organization invited another liberal in 2026.

Please don't misunderstand: The organization has every right to be as liberal as it wants to be. At its Chautauqua events, it has no obligation ever to give a non-liberal the time of day, much less invite a non-liberal to stand on its podium or behind its lectern.

You've read here about the organization's Chautauqua speakers in recent years.

The 2023 speaker disagreed with the Supreme Court's holding that race-based college and university admissions violate the Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause.

The 2024 speaker--whom Chautauqua Institution has invited to give a morning-amphitheater lecture in 2027--described non-liberal high-court results with words such as "madness," "hubris," "a lack of humility," "wildly disruptive," "outlandish," and "audacious."

The 2025 speaker said a 2000 high-court opinion was "the first time really that the Supreme Court made a decision that was just impossible to justify on the basis of its pre-existing law." Thus, the speaker believes (1) Dred Scott v. Sandford, the 1857 decision creating a right to own slaves where no such right had existed, and (2) Plessy v. Ferguson, the 1896 decision upholding racially-segregated public accommodations, were possible for the Supreme Court "to justify on the basis of its pre-existing law."

Then came 2026, when the speaker was a veteran of two investigations of President Trump 45. Although that doesn't reveal the speaker's perspective, those hoping for diversity of thought could have suspected they were in for disappointment when the speaker prefaced thoughts on three topics with this: "It's well to remember the Supreme Court's potential for fallibility and the chance for correction at times like these when the court's decisions can engender intense controversy."

local.title: Legislature rejects benefit change for managers
local.summary: MAYVILLE – After a couple of months of indecision, county lawmakers have rejected a proposal to have managers get the same retirement insurance benefits as union employees. Back in September, the Chautauqua County Legislature looked at modifying a local law that would permit a retiring manager to “r
local.body:
MAYVILLE - After a couple of months of indecision, county lawmakers have rejected a proposal to have managers get the same retirement insurance benefits as union employees.

Back in September, the Chautauqua County Legislature looked at modifying a local law that would permit a retiring manager to "receive paid health insurance coverage after retirement at the rate which matches that of the highest service-related calculation afforded within any county union collective bargaining unit agreement."

At both the September and October legislature meetings, county supervisors spoke out, saying that there have been times when union employees were declining promotions simply because the union benefits were better than what they would get as a supervisor. Others said that managers had left their supervisory role to rejoin the union later in their careers, simply because of the benefits the union members get in retirement.

In both September and October, the legislature sent the change to the local law back to committee for further discussion.

During Wednesday night's county legislature meeting, Legislator Tom Nelson, D-Jamestown, said he supported the change. "First, I think it’s important to provide competitive benefits to attract and retain qualified management employees. Second, I believe we should recognize the years of service our management employees have given to the county. But mostly I support this because it protects benefits earned in union positions. Many of our county employees spent years serving the county beginning in union positions before moving into management," he said.

But Legislator Fred Johnson, R-Westfield, disagreed. "What Legislator Nelson was talking about is the heart of a good comp and benefits policy and strategy. This is not the way to go about it. ... If we have a compensation issue at any part of our employees relative to the marketplace, then let’s deal with it in a professional manner. But cherry-picking a particular benefit and then just running it across the management group is not a way to go about this," he said.

The local law as written did not specify what the potential cost would be. That bothered Legislator Chuck Nazzaro, D-Jamestown, who was sworn into office in October. "I’ve not heard the cost to the county," he said.

During various committee meetings, there had been talk about what the potential costs would be, but that was never made clear.

local.title: Buffalo woman charged after feds seize 27 pounds of drugs, loaded handgun
local.summary: A woman has been charged after federal authorities seized more than 27 pounds of drugs, cash and a loaded handgun from a Buffalo home on Thursday.
local.body: A woman has been charged after federal authorities seized more than 27 pounds of drugs, cash and a loaded handgun from a Buffalo home on Thursday.Authorities said the seizure happened at 231 Comstock Avenue, where they found approximately 22 pounds of fentanyl, five pounds of cocaine and an additional quantity of methamphetamine.Keona Goins, 48, of Buffalo, was charged by federal criminal complaint with possession with intent to distribute fentanyl and cocaine. The charges carry a maximum potential sentence of 20 years in prison.Neighbors describe the area as generally quiet. Trinity Dunkin, who lives in the neighborhood, said, "For the most part, it's quiet on these streets."But federal investigators said the alleged drug activity could have had serious consequences for the community."The alleged criminal activity poisons our communities, fuels violence, endangers the vulnerable, ultimately putting lives at risk," said Anthony Patron, special agent in charge with Homeland Security Investigations.U.S. Attorney Michael DiGiacomo said the investigation was part of the Homeland Security Task Force initiative, a government partnership focused on disrupting criminal organizations."This investigation is part of the Homeland Security Task Force initiative, which is a government partnership focused on eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, human smuggling and trafficking rings all operating here in the United States and abroad," DiGiacomo said.The investigation involved several federal, state and local agencies, including Homeland Security Investigations, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, the FBI, Buffalo Police and the Niagara County Sheriff's Office.DiGiacomo said authorities intend to continue pursuing drug trafficking investigations."The message is very simple. If you choose to traffic narcotics in this district or this community, you will face the combined efforts of law enforcement and prosecution. It's that simple," DiGiacomo said.For Dunkin, the seizure is a relief."I'm glad they found it before it got worse," she said.DiGiacomo said federal prosecutors will continue using every lawful tool available to investigate and prosecute those accused of trafficking dangerous drugs.

local.title: SUNY enrollment grows for fourth straight year, but Buffalo State, Fredonia continue to struggle
local.summary: SUNY enrollment is up for the fourth year in a row, but some Western New York campuses aren't seeing the same growth.
local.body: Enrollment across the State University of New York (SUNY) system is growing for the fourth consecutive year, reversing a long-running trend of declining student populations. But not every Western New York campus is sharing in that success.SUNY Chancellor Dr. John King says the system now has 392,401 students, an increase of 1.3% from last year and up nearly 8% since 2022.In an interview with 7 News, Dr. King credited the turnaround to the affordability of SUNY schools, increased state funding and new programs designed to attract adult learners."I think New Yorkers are seeing the affordable excellence that is available at SUNY," Dr. King said. "Our four-year institutions, the tuition for a full year is $7,070. That's incredibly affordable compared to private colleges, compared to other public systems."Dr. King said the growth is particularly significant because it follows years of declining enrollment."Not only is it four years in a row of growth across every sector, but this is really the first time we've had that in at least 25 years," he said.While enrollment is increasing statewide, the picture is more complicated at colleges and universities in Western New York.Enrollment at the University at Buffalo remained relatively flat this year, despite challenges involving international students.SUNY Erie and most other community colleges are also seeing encouraging results, particularly through the state's SUNY Reconnect program.But Buffalo State University and SUNY Fredonia continue to experience enrollment declines."I continue to worry about Buffalo State and Fredonia," Dr. King told 7 News. entertainment.title: Yo, Academy! When ‘Rocky’ Was Crowned Best Picture Champ
entertainment.summary: Fifty years ago, Sylvester Stallone’s movie about an underdog boxer toppled films like ‘Taxi Driver’ and ‘All the President’s Men’ at the Oscars.
entertainment.body:
If you want to know the behind-the-scenes story of how Sylvester Stallone got Rocky into theaters, check out I Play Rocky , opening nationwide Nov. 20, just one day shy of the original film’s 50th anniversary. How Stallone typed up a screenplay in just a few days. How he waved away piles of money in order to star in the picture himself, despite the studio insisting on a bigger name (like, say, Burt Reynolds, Ryan O’Neal or Clint Eastwood). How shooting that beef-beating scene in the meat locker left Stallone with bloody fists and busted knuckles. All that and more is faithfully re-enacted in Peter Farrelly’s new backstage biopic. Related Stories Movies Golden Globes Category Chaos: When 'The Drama' Is a Comedy... Movies IDFA: 'The Year of the Ghost' and 'Memories of Lightning' Win Amsterdam Doc Fest Awards

What’s not in the film, though, is what happened after Rocky ‘s Nov. 21, 1976, New York opening, which in some ways is just as incredible an underdog story. With no stars (except Burgess Meredith) and virtually no budget (even 50 years ago, a million dollars was a pittance in Hollywood), Rocky had no business becoming the biggest film of the year. But it ended up drawing blockbuster crowds — with audiences cheering as if ringside at a real boxing match — ultimately grossing $225 million worldwide, or about $1.3 billion in today’s dollars.

Then there was round two, Oscar night. At the 49th Academy Awards , Rocky beat Network , Taxi Driver , All the President’s Men and Bound for Glory for best picture, and also picked up a best director statuette for John G. Avildsen. Stallone himself went home empty-handed, as did his three nominated co-stars, Talia Shire, Meredith and Burt Young. But he got the night’s most memorable moment: Muhammad Ali crashed the stage while Stallone was presenting and traded a few fake punches.

entertainment.title: The morbid way Robert Pattinson celebrated his James Bond casting revealed
entertainment.summary: Pattinson got the offer to play the next James Bond on Sunday, but the news didn't go public until the next day.
entertainment.body:
Robert Pattinson was watching a gothic horror film when the world learned he’s the new James Bond.

Robert Eggers, Pattinson’s longtime friend and collaborator, told Variety the “Twilight” actor was screening his upcoming movie “Werwulf” when the news broke on Monday.

Ironically, “Werwulf,” which follows a ravenous beast haunting a 14th-century English town, stars Aaron Taylor-Johnson, an early favorite to replace Daniel Craig as the spy agent.

Eggers, who worked with Pattinson on the 2019 horror film “The Lighthouse,” told IGN he was “not surprised” that the British actor was cast as Bond.

“I was just texting him about it this morning,” Eggers also shared.

When asked how Pattinson felt about “Werwulf,” Eggers replied, “Oh, he loved it, of course.”

Pattinson was officially offered the role of Bond on a Sunday phone call, but the news didn’t become public until the next day, according to Variety.

Amazon MGM Studios, which bought the rights to the Bond franchise from the Broccoli family last year, spent between $300,000 and $500,000 on screen tests for the new Bond movie, Variety reported.

entertainment.title: ‘Best Pancakes in the County’ Review: Nicolas Cage Goes Gonzo, Again, in a Dismal Action-Comedy That Fails to Match His Energy
entertainment.summary: A remote diner is the setting for Ken Sanzel's movie featuring a stand-off between corrupt FBI agents and a gang of criminals.
entertainment.body:
You have to admire Nicolas Cage ’s penchants for loyalty and consistency. His latest effort reunites him with director-screenwriter Ken Sanzel, with whom he previously collaborated on 2019’s Kill Chain , a film that few saw and even fewer liked. And it features the sort of gonzo trademark Cage performance for which he’s become both admired and ridiculed, in this case featuring a degree of misplaced commitment to the bit that definitely doesn’t pay off. The only saving grace of Best Pancakes in the County is the excellent recipe advice about the titular food that will definitely improve your breakfast gatherings. Related Stories Movies Nicolas Cage on His Approach to Playing John Madden in New Biopic: "I'm Not an Impressionist" Movies 'Madden' Review: Nicolas Cage and Christian Bale Go for Broke in a Cartoonish Biopic From David O. Russell That's Strictly for Football Fanatics

This is the sort of movie that is routinely described as “Tarantinoesque” (a word that’s actually included in the Oxford English Dictionary, don’t you know) thanks to its convoluted plotting, eccentric characters, jokey dialogue, and propensity for Mexican standoffs. These movies are, with a few exceptions, invariably bad, but this one takes the pancake. Best Pancakes in the County The Bottom Line The worst movie in the multiplex. Release date : Friday, November 20 Cast : Nicolas Cage, Justin Long, Shelley Hennig, Ravi Patel, Brandon Mychal Smith, Lauren German, Kelly Greyson Director-screenwriter : Ken Sanzel 1 hour 38 minutes

Cage clearly participated in creating the look for his character, labeled in an onscreen graphic as “The Son of a Bitch.” Playing a ruthless criminal who doesn’t hesitate to shoot his partner while eating ice cream after a safe-cracking burglary goes awry, the actor wears hideous ‘70s-era clothes and a terrible perm wig, his make-up featuring extensive facial scarring and a porcine nose. He also employs a speaking style that sounds like he inhaled helium before every take.

Cage, absent from the proceedings for long stretches, gives it all and then some, to the point that you can feel his delight upon repeatedly uttering the phrase “I can’t find my thumb!” after a particularly gruesome incident. You half expect him to reprise his line “I’m Nicolas friggin’ Cage!” from The Unbearable Weight of Massive Talent .

His efforts, as gonzo as they are, are all for naught, with the movie’s incoherent plotting, risible dialogue, and subpar filmmaking making it a torturous experience with nothing memorable about it other than its title. That the distributor doesn’t have much confidence in its prospects is evident from its simultaneous release in “select” theaters and availability on digital platforms.

entertainment.title: Battle to keep James Bond auditions secret cost Amazon a huge sum
entertainment.summary: Amazon executives did not spare any expense during their years-long search, according to new reports. On Monday, it was finally announced that Robert Pattinson officially landed the role.
entertainment.body:
The hunt for a new James Bond seems to have left Amazon MGM’s wallet shaken and stirred.

Executives working on the latest installment in the spy thriller franchise are said to have forked out hundreds of thousands of dollars in an attempt to keep their grueling search for a new 007 under wraps, according to Variety .

Robert Pattinson was officially announced as the latest James Bond on Monday — but not before multiple A-list actors took part in screen tests for the role, a process that reportedly cost Amazon MGM up to $500,000.

While the studio officially bought the rights to James Bond in 2025 for $20 million, the search by an A-list team of producers did not kick off until earlier this year.

Famed “Spider-Man” producer Amy Pascal and David Heyman, who worked on the “Harry Potter” movies, initially held screen tests with actors including Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, and Josh O’Connor.

During this time, Amazon MGM spent “between $300,000 and $500,000” to keep the screen tests secret, multiple sources told Variety — a price that some might argue was essentially wasted.

Though much effort was made to keep the auditions under wraps, the actors’ names quickly became public knowledge as speculation reached fever pitch.

Pattinson then tested for the role at the last minute, as did fellow wildcard Nicholas Hoult .

entertainment.title: Hailey Bieber gets candid about suicidal thoughts she had during intense Selena Gomez feud
entertainment.summary: "I was going through a time where people were yelling at me in the street," the model heartbreakingly recalled.
entertainment.body:
Hailey Bieber thought “it would be better if [she] wasn’t here anymore” at the height of her feud with Selena Gomez .

“I had people telling me to kill myself in the comments every single day. I was going through a time where people were yelling at me in the street,” the Rhode founder shared during her panel at the New York Times’ DealBook Summit in New York on Wednesday.

“People were putting tip jars up in Starbucks of me versus this person,” the model recalled, referring to Gomez, who had an on-again, off-again relationship with her husband, Justin Bieber, for nearly a decade.

Hailey admitted that she was “too sensitive” to ignore the hate she was getting online, and that dark thoughts began to creep in.

“I had never experienced anything like that before. So the way that people were making me feel was that maybe it would be better if I wasn’t here anymore,” she continued. “Because that’s how intense I felt other people’s feelings were towards me at the time.”

Nowadays, the beauty mogul tries to “regulate” how much time she spends on social media, though she confessed it is “tough to try to limit yourself” since the platforms are “so available.”

Hailey added that she continues to “deal with comparison” and can feel insecure when looking at others on the internet. The mom of one said she never wants to hide her insecurities in hopes of having future discussions with her kids about the dangers of social media.

“I want to be able to have [that conversation] with my kids so that when they’re feeling that way, they can relate to mom,” she shared, “and know that I feel that way too sometimes and we can be in that together.”

She will also oversee a team of project managers for marketing, commerce, distribution, DSP and streaming.

Victor-Burkhardt previously served as senior vp, head of publicity and brand strategy at Epic Records, where she worked with clients including Future, Travis Scott, 21 Savage, Giveon, Mariah The Scientist, Madison Beer and Zara Larsson.
